description.value: We examined the cognitive reappraisal of positive and negative affect in healthy younger and older adults, and the neural correlates of reappraisal among older adults.

spans.text: We examined the cognitive reappraisal of positive and negative affect in healthy younger and older adults, and the neural correlates of reappraisal among older adults.

value: We predicted that older adults would be less effective at regulating positive (based on socioemotional selectivity theory and motivation to maintain positive affect) and negative emotions (consistent with past literature) using CR compared to young adults (behaviorally).

Because older adults tend to engage in CR more than young adults, we hypothesized that older adults would engage canonical reappraisal-related regions (e.g. DLPFC and DMPFC) and less canonical, compensatory regions (e.g. VMPFC) during CR compared to a non-regulation/attend condition.

Because older adults tend to be less successful at engaging in CR than young adults, we predicted they would show noticeable, but small declines in activity in emotion appraisal regions (e.g. amygdala, insula).
In general, we predicted larger effects (i.e. more effective regulation and more engagement of CR regions) for negatively valenced conditions based on socioemotional selectivity theory.
we hypothesized that older adults would be less motivated to downregulate positive affect relative to negative affect.
